newsitem.title: UK: British children getting big and fat, study finds.
newsitem.headline: British children getting big and fat, study finds.

text.p: British children are growing taller -- which used to be taken as a sign of good health and nutrition -- but they are also getting fatter, researchers reported on Wednesday.
Children in general are around 20 percent fatter than they were in 1972, John Hughes of St Thomas's Hospital in London found.
He examined height and weight of more than 10,000 English and Scottish children aged between five and 11 gathered in surveys between 1972 and 1994.
Scottish children were on average two cm taller (just under an inch) while English children gained 1.5 cm (half an inch) in average height.
Upper-arm measurements, seen as pointing to fatness, also increased in all children.

Nine-year-old Scottish boys were 24 percent fatter in 1994 than in 1972 while 10-year-old Scottish girls were 22 percent fatter. English boys were 17 percent fatter. Only English girls did not gain significantly -- they were 2.5 to seven percent fatter.
"The increases...do not augur well for targets in the reduction of obesity," Hughes wrote in the Archives of Disease in Childhood.
Last week, a survey published in the British Medical Journal found children were walking less because of parental fears over their safety.

And in his annual survey on the state of the nation's health released last month, Chief Medical Officer Kenneth Calman said 15 percent of British men and 16.5 percent of women aged between 16 and 64 were obese.
This compared to 12.7 percent of men and 15 percent of women in 1991. In 1980 only six percent of men were obese.
